performers: María Barrientos, soprano; Manuel de Falla, piano
intro: María Barrientos sings the fourth of the Seven Popular Spanish Songs with the composer at the piano, recorded for Columbia in Paris in 1928. A long piano introduction in 3/8 comes first; then a lover takes his leave: goodbye, my girl, until tomorrow.

sections.label: A · First couplet, “They say we do not love”
Link · The piano returns to the opening pace
Coda · Tranquillo, the voice far off

cues.title: Piano alone, in three-eight
cues.text: The piano begins alone, pianissimo, in 3/8 at Allegro vivo. Quick turning figures sit above repeated chords marked staccato sempre, and the voice waits through a long introduction.
cues.evidence: Falla, Siete canciones populares españolas (Max Eschig, 1922), no. 4, printed pages 15–16: 3/8, Allegro vivo (dotted crotchet = 92), pianissimo, “stacc. sempre”; the voice enters at the change to 3/4. https://archive.org/details/sietecancionespo00fall
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The voice enters
cues.text: The metre changes to 3/4, Poco meno vivo, and the soprano takes the first couplet: they say we do not love each other, because they never see us talk; let them ask your heart and mine.
cues.evidence: Eschig 1922 edition, no. 4, printed pages 16–17: Poco meno vivo, 3/4, the voice entering on “Dicen que no nos queremos / porque no nos ven hablar; a tu corazón y al mío / se lo pueden preguntar”. https://archive.org/details/sietecancionespo00fall
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Falla at the piano
cues.text: The pianist is the composer. Columbia recorded María Barrientos with Falla in Paris on 31 March 1928, and the Jota was issued on the French Columbia disc PFX-1.
cues.evidence: Discography of American Historical Recordings, Columbia matrix WLX310: Jota, soprano with piano, María Barrientos and Manuel de Falla; recorded 31 March 1928, Paris; issued on Columbia (France/Belgium) PFX-1. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/detail/2000434595/WLX310-Jota

cues.title: The farewell couplet
cues.text: After the piano returns to the opening pace, the second couplet begins: “Ya me despido de ti” — I take my leave of you, of your house and your window; and even if your mother objects, goodbye, my girl, until tomorrow.
cues.evidence: Eschig 1922 edition, no. 4, printed pages 18–20: Iº Tempo (Allegro vivo) for the piano, then the second text beginning “Ya me despido de ti” and ending “Adiós, niña, hasta mañana”. https://archive.org/details/sietecancionespo00fall
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Tranquillo, the voice far off
cues.text: The last page slows to Tranquillo (crotchet = 76). The soprano, marked “lontano”, murmurs “even if your mother does not wish it”, and the piano fades through a rit. molto to triple piano.
cues.evidence: Eschig 1922 edition, no. 4, printed page 21: Tranquillo (crotchet = 76), “pp lontano” over the words “Aunque no quiera tu madre”, “rit. molto”, ppp. https://archive.org/details/sietecancionespo00fall
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: DAHR lists both as personnel for matrix WLX310; the Archivo Manuel de Falla credits them together for the cycle in its 2021 exhibition.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Voice and piano, the fourth song of the cycle
fields.note: DAHR describes the recording as soprano vocal solo with piano. The published edition used and the key sung are not stated in the sources consulted.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: DAHR gives 31 March 1928 for matrix WLX310 from Michael Gray’s compilation of the Columbia recording logs. The Archivo Manuel de Falla’s 2021 exhibition credits give 1930 for other songs of the cycle (Nana, Asturiana), and a 2022 review dates the whole recording between 1928 and 1930.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: DAHR cites Copeland for the recording location; the studio is not named.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Twelve-inch 78-rpm disc; the Internet Archive item gives the publisher as French Columbia.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: DAHR lists the Jota under Columbia (France/Belgium) PFX-1; the second file of the Internet Archive item is named for Columbia PFX-1.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: The transfer is a single side lasting 3:05; which face of PFX-1 carries the Jota is not stated.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: Item in the Internet Archive’s 78-rpm opera collection; no personal mastering credit is given.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item was uploaded on 22 November 2019; the date of the transfer itself is not stated.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Digitised at 78 rpm; stylus size “40e” as stated in the item
fields.note: Equalisation, noise reduction and any restoration settings are not stated.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Falla died on 14 November 1946. Spanish law protects the works of authors who died before 7 December 1987 for life plus 80 years, so his music remains protected in Spain until the end of 2026; arrangements and modern editions carry their own rights
fields.note: A phonogram term assessment does not clear the composition, an arrangement or a modern score edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU phonogram public-domain basis: issued on Columbia PFX-1 in or after mid-1930, a 78-rpm disc, before 1963
fields.note: DAHR places the session in March 1928 and the disc in Columbia’s French catalogue (PFX-1). The Marston track list for its Supervia volume 5 pairs the Jota (matrix WLX 310, 31 March 1928) on PFX-1 with Nana and Canción (WLX 1368, recorded 3 June 1930), so the disc cannot have appeared before mid-1930; the Archivo Manuel de Falla’s credits give 1930 for other songs of the cycle. No dated advertisement, review or catalogue giving the issue date of PFX-1 was found. The Marston restoration of the Jota runs 3:08 against 3:05 here, so this transfer may run slightly fast. This is a territorial phonogram basis, not US or worldwide clearance and not a Creative Commons licence.

composer.background:
As a boy in Cádiz, Manuel de Falla governed a city of his own. Colón had a council, newspapers and a theatre, and according to Roland-Manuel’s 1930 biography the triumph of the day there was El conde de Villamediana, an opera seria composed and conducted by a certain Manuel de Falla. He kept the city running for six years. The real boy was born on 23 November 1876 at 3 Plaza de Mina and meant to be a writer. At seventeen, he told Roland-Manuel in 1928, a conviction at once timid and deep sent him towards composition.

In Madrid he studied the piano with José Tragó and won the conservatoire’s first prize in 1899. Two years later he asked the Catalan musicologist Felipe Pedrell to teach him; from Pedrell, he told his biographer Jaime Pahissa, came the clearest and most solid guidance for his work.
